notes: Ruling slot 18 = UPC (Obote). Coalition slot 19 = the 'Move to the Left' ideologues of the Common Man's Charter (Oct 1969) inside the UPC. Opposition parties (DP, KY) proscribed after the 19 Dec 1969 attempt on Obote. Slot 0 = Amin's army network (pro-British/Israeli), slot 22 = Uganda Army as institution. Kabaka Mutesa II died in London Nov 1969; heir Ronald Mutebi in exile.

0.name: Askari wa Amin
0.text:
Around Major-General Idi Amin, commander of the army and air force, has grown a personal network of West Nile officers, Kakwa, Lugbara and Nubian recruits, and paratroopers trained with Israeli help. Amin, decorated hero of the 1966 assault on the Kabaka's palace, is now distrusted by Obote and watched by the General Service Unit.

The network speaks Swahili, the language of the barracks, and looks to London and Tel Aviv rather than to Moscow. It has little interest in the Common Man's Charter and much in promotions, arms and the Sudanese border. Its leverage lies in loyal battalions in Kampala and Jinja.

1.name: Democratic Party
1.text:
The Democratic Party was founded in 1954 and led Uganda's first internal self-government under Benedicto Kiwanuka in 1961. After the attempt on Obote's life in December 1969 it was proscribed together with all other opposition parties, and Kiwanuka is in detention.

The DP draws on Catholic Uganda: mission schools, catechists and Baganda and western farmers who resent the Protestant establishment. It stands for constitutional government, multiparty elections, private property and close ties to the West and the Vatican. Its leverage lies in the parishes, which no decree can dissolve.

2.name: Uganda Law Society
2.text:
The Uganda Law Society is the professional body of the country's advocates, many of them Makerere and London trained, a sizeable share of them Asian. Since the 1966 crisis, the suspension of the independence constitution and the detentions under emergency regulations, it has become one of the few remaining voices for due process.

Its members argue for an independent judiciary, habeas corpus, free courts for detainees and a press without censorship. They distrust both the Common Man's Charter and the army. The society has no mass base, but its lawyers defend the detained and keep the language of rights alive.

3.name: Uganda Labour Congress
3.text:
The Uganda Labour Congress is the main trade-union centre, built in the 1950s with the support of the Western-oriented ICFTU. Its veteran leader Humphrey Luande sits as a UPC member of parliament, yet the government increasingly wants unions as instruments of national development rather than as bargaining partners.

The congress organizes railwaymen, sugar and cotton workers, plantation labour and civil servants. It wants collective bargaining, a minimum wage and Africanization of skilled jobs, but resists state control of the unions. Its leverage lies in the railway, the Owen Falls power station and the Jinja industries.

4.name: Uganda People's Congress Youth League
4.text:
The UPC Youth League was the radical engine of the ruling party in the early 1960s, the base of former secretary-general John Kakonge, and a recruiting ground for students sent to Moscow, Prague and Sofia. Purged after Kakonge's fall in 1964, it has revived with the turn to the left in 1969.

Its cadres want a vanguard party, nationalization of the commanding heights, state farms and close ties with the Soviet bloc. They distrust Asian commerce, Buganda's notables and the army. The league's leverage lies in rallies, party branches and the returning graduates of Eastern European universities.

5.name: Makerere University Students' Guild
5.text:
Makerere University College, part of the University of East Africa, is the intellectual centre of the region. Its Students' Guild has moved left with the debates around Transition magazine, Dar es Salaam radicalism and the Vietnam war.

Guild radicals denounce neo-colonialism, Asian commercial dominance and the Western companies in copper and sugar, but also the authoritarian turn of the UPC state. They demand free speech on campus, African socialism with real participation and solidarity with liberation movements in southern Africa. Their leverage lies in demonstrations, pamphlets and the future elite they represent.

6.name: Rwenzururu
6.text:
The Rwenzururu movement arose in 1962 among the Bakonzo and Baamba of the Rwenzori mountains against domination by the Toro kingdom. Its leader Isaya Mukirania has proclaimed himself king and runs a rebel administration in the high valleys, beyond the reach of the army and the police.

The movement rejects Kampala, Fort Portal and every outside authority, collects its own taxes and keeps its own courts. It wants a separate district or kingdom for the mountain peoples and a return to customary order. Its leverage lies in mountain terrain, popular loyalty and the government's inability to end a costly insurgency.

7.name: General Service Unit
7.text:
The General Service Unit is Obote's personal intelligence service, created outside the police and the army and headed by his cousin Akena Adoko. After the December 1969 assassination attempt it has expanded its informers across Buganda, the civil service and the barracks.

The GSU is the shield of the Move to the Left: it watches the opposition, the Kabaka's loyalists, Asian traders and above all Idi Amin. It favours a one-party state ruled from the President's office, detention without trial and a security apparatus independent of the army. Its leverage lies in files, informers and Obote's trust.

8.name: Shia Imami Ismaili Community of Uganda
8.english: Shia Imami Ismaili Community of Uganda
8.text:
The Ismaili community of Uganda, followers of the Aga Khan, is one of the best organized Asian groups in the country, with jamatkhanas in Kampala, Jinja and Mbale and a network of schools, hospitals and cooperative banks. Prince Karim Aga Khan guides it through councils of lay leaders.

The community favours education, women's advancement, economic self-help and loyalty to the state of residence. It looks warily at the Common Man's Charter and the push for Africanization of trade. Its leverage lies in capital, professional skills and an international network reaching from Nairobi to Karachi and London.

9.name: Khoja Shia Ithna-Asheri Jamaat of Kampala
9.english: Khoja Shia Ithna-Asheri Jamaat of Kampala
9.text:
The Khoja Shia Ithna-Asheri Jamaat of Kampala unites the Twelver Shia merchants who broke away from the Ismailis in the late 19th century. It belongs to the Africa Federation of Khoja Shia Ithna-Asheri Jamaats and follows the great clerical authorities of Najaf.

The jamaat insists on religious law, the authority of the marja and strict communal discipline, and sends its young men to study in Iraq. Its members fear nationalization and the rising hostility to Asian commerce. Its leverage lies in trade, mosque endowments and ties to Shia centres in Iraq and Iran.

10.name: Uganda Muslim Community
10.text:
The Uganda Muslim Community, based at Kibuli hill in Kampala, is led by Prince Badru Kakungulu, a member of the Buganda royal family and the most respected Muslim leader in the country. It runs mosques, schools and the Kibuli hospital.

Kibuli stands for Sunni orthodoxy, respect for the Kabaka's heritage and Muslim unity under traditional leadership. It refuses to be absorbed by Obote's rival Muslim association and keeps its distance from the UPC. Its leverage lies in Kakungulu's prestige, Buganda's Muslim gentry and links to Egypt and Saudi Arabia.

11.name: Ansar as-Sunna
11.text:
Ansar as-Sunna is a small circle of preachers among the Nubian and West Nile Muslims, inspired by the Sudanese movement of the same name and by graduates returning from Medina. It meets in back-street mosques of Kampala, Arua and Bombo.

Its members denounce Sufi practices, saint veneration and the compromises of the established sheikhs, and dream of a single Muslim community governed by sharia across the Nile valley. They have no political organization, but their sermons find listeners among soldiers and traders in the north. Their leverage lies in Sudanese contacts and in Nubian garrison towns.

12.name: National Association for the Advancement of Muslims
12.english: National Association for the Advancement of Muslims
12.text:
The National Association for the Advancement of Muslims was founded in 1965 with UPC backing to pull Muslims away from Kibuli and the Buganda establishment. It is led by Adoko Nekyon, Obote's cousin and a minister, and controls much of the state money for Muslim schools.

NAAM preaches Muslim advancement through education, loyalty to the republic and cooperation with the government's socialist programme. Its opponents call it a government front. Its leverage lies in state patronage, Muslims outside Buganda and its claim to speak for the community in dealings with the Arab world.

13.name: Uganda Development Corporation
13.text:
The Uganda Development Corporation is the state's industrial holding, created in 1952 and owner or partner in textiles, cement, hotels, tea estates and the Kilembe copper mine. Its managers and planners are the technocratic arm of government.

The UDC favours planned industrialization, import substitution and state partnership with foreign capital rather than ideological nationalization. It is the natural instrument for the Common Man's Charter yet wary of party interference. Its leverage lies in budgets, contracts, jobs and the expertise the government cannot do without.

14.name: Church of Uganda
14.text:
The Church of Uganda is the Anglican province of Uganda, Rwanda and Burundi, led since 1966 by Erica Sabiti, its first African archbishop. Protestant Uganda has long supplied the colonial chiefs, the senior civil servants and many UPC leaders.

The church stands for Christian family life, mission schools, hospitals and moral order, and is wary of both radical socialism and Catholic political ambitions. It is divided between Buganda and the other dioceses. Its leverage lies in parishes across the country, the school system and the Protestant identity of much of the ruling elite.

15.name: Madhvani Group
15.text:
The Madhvani Group, built from the Kakira sugar works near Jinja, is the largest private industrial empire in East Africa, with sugar, steel, textiles, glass and edible oils. It is headed by Jayant Madhvani, a respected figure in Kampala's business world and close to government circles.

The group wants stable property rights, protected markets and partnership with the state rather than nationalization. It employs thousands of Africans and many Asians and finances charities and schools. Its leverage lies in sugar, foreign exchange and the government's dependence on its output and tax payments.

16.name: Uganda Chamber of Commerce
16.text:
The Uganda Chamber of Commerce represents traders, importers, cotton ginners and coffee exporters, many of them Asian, alongside a growing number of African businessmen in Kampala and the district towns.

The chamber argues for free trade, low taxes, open import licensing and the protection of private enterprise. It opposes state trading corporations, price controls and the nationalization plans implicit in the Common Man's Charter. Its leverage lies in the retail and export trade on which the economy and the treasury depend.

17.name: Uganda National Parks
17.text:
Uganda National Parks, founded in 1952, administers Murchison Falls and Queen Elizabeth national parks, with their elephants, hippos and tree-climbing lions. Its trustees and wardens work with Makerere zoologists and foreign conservation societies.

The parks fight poaching, cattle grazing inside protected land and plans for a hydroelectric dam on the Nile at Murchison Falls. Their case is that wildlife tourism earns foreign exchange a poor country cannot spare. Their leverage lies in international donors, the tourist trade and the prestige of Uganda's wildlife abroad.

18.name: Uganda People's Congress
18.text:
The Uganda People's Congress, founded in 1960, has ruled since independence under Milton Obote. After abolishing the kingdoms in 1967 and surviving an assassination attempt in December 1969, it is now the only legal party. Obote has proclaimed the Common Man's Charter as its programme.

The UPC promises a Move to the Left: an end to tribal and feudal privilege, state control of key industries, Africanization of commerce and a single national party. It is non-aligned, friendly with Tanzania and wary of Britain. Its base lies in the north, Lango and Acholi, and among Protestant elites, civil servants and party branches.

19.name: Move to the Left
19.text:
The Move to the Left is the circle of ideologues and ministers around the President's office who drafted the Common Man's Charter in 1969. They see the UPC not as a coalition of notables but as the instrument of a socialist transformation guided from State House.

They want the state to take majority shares in banks, oil companies and industry, a single party linking leaders and masses, and an end to the political power of chiefs, kings and merchants. They admire Nyerere's Arusha Declaration and keep equal distance from both blocs. Their leverage lies in Obote's backing and control of policy.

20.name: Kabaka Yekka
20.text:
Kabaka Yekka, 'the King Alone', was founded in 1961 as the political movement of Buganda's loyalists and formed the first independence government in alliance with the UPC. It collapsed after the 1966 attack on the palace and the flight of Kabaka Mutesa II, who died in London in November 1969.

Its surviving followers demand the restoration of the kingdom, federal status for Buganda and the return of the royal heir. They regard Obote as a usurper. Their leverage lies in Buganda's numbers, the wealth of Kampala and a deep popular grievance.

21.name: Abalwanirizi ba Buganda
21.text:
The Abalwanirizi ba Buganda are the underground militants of Buganda nationalism: former palace guards, embittered young men from Mengo and Kampala's suburbs, and exiles in Nairobi and London. The gunman who wounded Obote at Lugogo stadium on 19 December 1969 came from this milieu.

They reject compromise with the republic and see violence as the only road back to the kingdom. They dream of an independent Buganda ruled by its king and purged of northern soldiers. Their leverage lies in secrecy, Buganda's anger and the regime's fear of further attacks.

22.name: Uganda Army
22.text:
The Uganda Army grew out of the King's African Rifles and was expanded rapidly after the 1964 mutiny. Commanded by Idi Amin, it put down the Buganda resistance in 1966 and now underpins the Obote regime. Its officers are divided between Acholi and Langi on one side and West Nile on the other.

The army demands budgets, equipment and promotions and sees itself as the guardian of national unity. Its leaders are drawn to British and Israeli training missions rather than to the Soviet bloc. Its leverage lies in the barracks of Kampala, Jinja and Bombo and in its role as Obote's indispensable support.

23.name: Abalasangeye
23.text:
The Abalasangeye dynasty has ruled Buganda for centuries. Kabaka Mutesa II, first President of Uganda, was driven out in 1966 and died in exile in London in November 1969. His young heir, Ronald Muwenda Mutebi, lives in England, and the kingdom itself was abolished by the 1967 constitution.

The royal house remains the focus of Baganda identity. Its supporters want the kingdom restored, the Lukiiko revived and the Kabaka's lands returned. They look to Britain for sympathy. Their leverage lies in the loyalty of the Baganda, the clans and the memory of a dead king.
